title: What is an API?
text:
A Simple Analogy
Think of a restaurant.

You are the customer (your program)
The kitchen is the server (the service you want to use)
The waiter is the API

You do not walk into the kitchen and cook your own food. You tell the waiter what you want using the menu’s format “I’ll have the pasta, please.” The waiter takes that to the kitchen, and brings back a response the pasta.
The menu is the API. It defines exactly what you are allowed to ask for and what format to ask in.

title: What is an API?
text:
Why Do APIs Exist?
Imagine if every app had to build its own maps, its own payment system, its own weather data from scratch. That would be insane.
Instead, companies like Google, Stripe, and OpenAI build powerful services and expose them through APIs so that any developer in the world can use them in their own app without knowing anything about how the service works internally.
You just follow the menu.

Community Tools
Last lesson you built tools from scratch. That is an important skill but you do not always have to start from zero.
LangChain has a large library of community tools pre-built tools made by LangChain and the open source community that cover the most common things agents need to do.



Read This Before Class

As you read, for each tool ask yourself:

What does this tool do?

A New Challenge: Local Data
So far your agents have only worked with information from the internet or from their training. But in the real world, most of the data that matters lives in local files spreadsheets, CSVs, text documents, databases.
Getting an agent to work with local data requires a tool. Just like web search gives the agent access to the internet, a file-reading tool gives it access to your files.
Think about what that means: an agent that can search the web and read your internal files could answer questions like:

“Based on our sales data from last quarter, what does current market research say about our biggest product category?”

That is the kind of thing we will build toward in class.

text:
Part 2 Tool Descriptions Under Pressure
Last lesson you learned that the docstring is the agent’s instruction manual. That mattered when you had one tool. Now imagine you have four tools all available at once.
The agent has to read all four descriptions and pick the right one. If any description is vague, it will pick the wrong tool or get confused and pick none.


The Problem: Overlapping Tools
Here is a scenario with two tools that have bad descriptions:
@tool
def search_web(query: str) -> str:
    """Gets information."""  # ← too vague
    ...

@tool
def read_file(filename: str) -> str:
    """Gets information from a file."""  # ← still too vague
    ...
When the agent has both, it cannot tell which to use. “Gets information” describes almost everything.



The Fix: Specific, Mutually Exclusive Descriptions
@tool
def search_web(query: str) -> str:
    """
    Searches the internet for current information using DuckDuckGo.
    Use this tool when the user asks about recent events, current facts,
    or anything that may have changed recently.
    Do NOT use this for questions about our internal company data.
    """
    ...

@tool
def read_sales_data(query: str) -> str:
    """
    Reads and searches our internal sales CSV file.
    Use this tool when the user asks about our company's sales figures,
    customer counts, revenue, or product performance.
    Do NOT use this for general web searches or current events.
    """
    ...

Activity 2 Build a Local File Tool
Now you will build a tool that reads a local CSV file and makes that data accessible to the agent.

Step 1 Create the sample data file
Run this cell to create a small sales CSV file in your Colab environment:
# Create a sample sales data file
sample_data = """month,product,units_sold,revenue
January,Widget A,120,2400
January,Widget B,85,3400
February,Widget A,140,2800
February,Widget B,90,3600
March,Widget A,95,1900
March,Widget B,110,4400
April,Widget A,160,3200
April,Widget B,75,3000
"""

with open("sales_data.csv", "w") as f:
    f.write(sample_data)

print("sales_data.csv created!")



Step 2 Build the file reading tool
import csv
from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def read_sales_data(query: str) -> str:
    """
    Reads our internal sales data CSV file and returns relevant information.
    Use this tool when the user asks about sales figures, revenue, units sold,
    product performance, or any question about our company's internal sales data.
    Do NOT use this for general questions or current events   use web search for those.

    Args:
        query: A plain English description of what information you need from the sales data
    """
    try:
        with open("sales_data.csv", "r") as f:
            reader = csv.DictReader(f)
            rows = list(reader)

        # Return all the data as a readable string
        result = "Sales Data:\n"
        result += "month | product | units_sold | revenue\n"
        result += "-" * 45 + "\n"
        for row in rows:
            result += f"{row['month']} | {row['product']} | {row['units_sold']} | ${row['revenue']}\n"
        return result

    except FileNotFoundError:
        return "Error: sales_data.csv not found. Make sure the file exists."
Test it directly first:
print(read_sales_data.invoke({"query": "show me all sales data"}))



Step 3 Wire it into an agent
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from langchain.agents import create_react_agent

model = init_chat_model(
    model="google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash",
    temperature=0
)

system_prompt = """You are a sales data analyst assistant.
You have access to our internal sales data through your tool.
Use the read_sales_data tool whenever the user asks about sales, revenue, or product performance.
Answer in clear, plain English with specific numbers from the data."""

agent = create_react_agent(
    model=model,
    tools=[read_sales_data],
    prompt=system_prompt
)

response = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Which product made the most revenue overall?"}]})
print(response["messages"][-1].content)
Try these questions and observe:

"What month had the highest total revenue?"
"How many units of Widget A were sold in total?"
"Which product performed better on average?"








Important🛑 STOP HERE



Make sure your agent is reading from the file and answering correctly before moving to the next activity. If the answers look wrong, check that sales_data.csv was created in Step 1.

Activity 3 Combine Web Search + Local Data
Now the real challenge: give the agent both tools at once and make sure it picks the right one.
This is where your tool descriptions do the heavy lifting.
from langchain_community.tools import DuckDuckGoSearchRun

# Both tools available
search_tool = DuckDuckGoSearchRun()

# Give the agent both tools
agent = create_react_agent(
    model=model,
    tools=[search_tool, read_sales_data],
    prompt="""You are a business analyst assistant with two tools available:
1. A web search tool for current information from the internet
2. A sales data tool for our company's internal sales figures

Always choose the most appropriate tool for each question.
Use web search for general or current information.
Use the sales data tool for questions about our company's performance."""
)

# This should use the FILE tool
response = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What was our best selling month?"}]})
print("File question:", response["messages"][-1].content)

# This should use the SEARCH tool  
response = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What are current trends in widget manufacturing?"}]})
print("Search question:", response["messages"][-1].content)


The Pressure Test
Now deliberately try to break it. Ask questions that could go either way and see what the agent does:
# Ambiguous   which tool will it pick?
response = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "How are widgets selling?"}]})
print(response["messages"][-1].content)






NoteDiscuss with your partner




Did the agent pick the right tool for the ambiguous question?
What would you change in the tool descriptions to make it more reliable?
What does this tell you about how much the description matters when tools compete?





Improve the descriptions
Based on what you observed, try rewriting one or both tool descriptions to make the agent’s decision more reliable. Test again with the same ambiguous question.






TipThere is no perfect answer



Tool description writing is a skill like writing good instructions for a person. The goal is to iterate until the agent behaves the way you expect.

Artificial intelligence (AI) alignment is the process of encoding human values and goals into AI models to make them as helpful, safe and reliable as possible.

Honest: The model must provide accurate information, correctly calibrate and express its own uncertainty, and avoid deception or fabrication.

title: Outcomes
text:
Outcomes
Prompt, Context, Intent Engineering - Define context engineering - Explain why context engineering is needed to make a “good” agent - Identify the difference between prompt, context, and intent engineering - Plan multiple agentic systems without the use of a computer - Implement the three types of engineering within the agent system plan


Notes
Prep: short reading from LangChain Prep: case study on a “bad” agent - powerful but with poor intent. Possibly
Intent engineering vs. context engineering vs. prompt engineering
The meat. When do you need each, and are any of them irrelevant?
This day is spent with computers put away. Activities are class and group discussion related. Students design a few Agentic AI systems on whiteboard and compare with the class after each one.
Context engineering definition

“In every industrial-strength LLM app, context engineering is the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step. Science because doing this right involves task descriptions and explanations, few-shot examples, RAG, related (possibly multimodal) data, tools, state and history, compacting… Doing this well is highly non-trivial. And art because of the guiding intuition around LLM psychology of people spirits.” - Andrej Karpathy, OpenAI June 2024
Deepen understanding of “good” in the context of whether it works or not; identify failure modes
Deepen understanding of “good” in the context of whether it works or not; identify failure modes

Outcomes

Name the six failure modes, and say which lever fixes each
Classify an observed failure into a mode and defend the classification
Describe a failure along the three dimensions (silent/loud, isolated/cascading, model/code)
Recognize the same failure under other names, and explain why no taxonomy is authoritative

Notes
Start the conversation by asking what they expect from an agent, and what they would see as a failure. Collect their answers before showing the taxonomy — the list lands better as a tidying-up of what they already said than as a list handed down.
The taxonomy is committed in failure_modes.md. Teach from that document; it is the source of truth and holds the reasoning, the dropped categories, and the source links.

The framing that makes it teachable
The modes are named for the lever that fixes them, not for the phenomenon. So this is not a new list to memorize — it is the Module 1 build levers read backwards. Say that out loud early; it converts the whole day from vocabulary drill into recognition.








Mode
What went wrong
Lever




Tool
wrong tool, bad args, unparsed output
tool definitions & schemas


Grounding
asserts what nothing supports
retrieval / knowledge state


State
needed info lost, stale, or poisoned
state & memory design


Control
won’t stop, stops early, wanders
deterministic scaffolding


Specification
did what you said, not what you meant
instructions & spec


Safety
harmful or disallowed, even if correct
guardrails, permissions, HITL



Naming the mode is naming the fix. That is the whole point, and it is what makes the bridge competency (root-cause → choose a lever) teachable in a single day.


Admit the mess — out loud, early

No authoritative taxonomy exists. Every list is cut for a different purpose.
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps (2025) — cut by attacker. Mostly collapses into our Safety.
MAST (arxiv 2503.13657) — cut by trace analysis. 14 modes, multi-agent only.
Vendor lists — cut by what their tool detects. Five or six items, never the same six.
Ours is cut by the lever, because our question is “what do I change?”
Line to use: “Six because you need to say something in a meeting Tuesday. It’s a tool, not a discovery.”
Why say it: they’ll hit other lists this week, and Outcome 5 says an unhedged list in a four-year-old field is the warning sign.

If they push back that OWASP is authoritative — agree, then show the cut. It’s a risk register (what can hurt you); ours is a repair manual (what’s broken, indexed by the fix). No conflicts, because different axes. Work the mapping live:

4 of their 10 → our Safety alone (prompt injection, sensitive info disclosure, excessive agency, system prompt leakage). Our one lever, their whole field.
2 land outside our six (supply chain, model poisoning) — build-time, no lever a student can pull. Name it as a gap in ours, don’t paper over it.
Misinformation → Grounding. Unbounded consumption → Control. Improper output handling → Tool.
Two of ours have no OWASP entry: State and Specification. “Forgot the order number” and “did what I said, not what I meant” aren’t security risks — and they’re most of Project 2.
The point, sharper than “everyone disagrees”: the most authoritative list in the room is authoritative about a different question.
Detail worth using: LLM09 is “Misinformation,” not “hallucination.” OWASP dodged the popular word too.



Aliases — recognition, not memorization

Tool — tool interface / selection / execution error · parsing error · schema violation
Grounding — hallucination · fabrication · confabulation · faithfulness · sycophancy
State — context loss / exhaustion / degradation / rot · dumb zone · memory pollution
Control — infinite loop · budget drain · runaway · planning failure · premature termination
Specification — goal / semantic / spec drift · instruction decay · reward hacking
Safety — alignment violation · prompt injection · jailbreak · excessive agency · exfiltration

“Hallucination” is the most-used and least useful word. Follow-up is always: which lever?


The long list — hand out, don’t lecture
Job: make six feel like a compression of something real, not an arbitrary short list.
Tool — parsing error · wrong tool · bad args · never called · tool errored · too many tools · mis-framed descriptions Grounding — fabricated facts/citations/APIs · retrieval miss, answered anyway · retrieved and contradicted it · sycophantic confirmation State — window exhaustion · context degradation · memory pollution · session state loss Control — infinite loop · budget drain · premature termination · bad plan · abandons plan · wanders · sub-agent coordination loss · deadlock Specification — spec drift · semantic drift · hidden assumption · reward hacking Safety — prompt injection · excessive agency · data leak · alignment faking
Then the payoff: cascading errors and code bug are top-level modes on published lists and dimensions in ours. Taxonomies disagree about what counts as a category, not about what goes wrong.


The dimensions carry the real skill
Spend real time here, not just on the six.

silent ↔︎ loud — trains detection. A stack trace is a bug report; a confidently wrong refund amount is a diagnosis. Ask: “how would you have caught this if it never crashed?” Every evaluator they write later is an answer to that question.
isolated ↔︎ cascading — trains localization. Hunt the trace for the earliest bad span, not the last. This is the skill that makes their LangSmith reading from 2_2 pay off.
model ↔︎ code — students reflexively blame the model. Separate it early.



Coverage note
slide2_3.qmd works three of the six in depth — Control (infinite loop), Tool (hallucinated planning), Safety (unsafe tool use). Grounding, State, and Specification are named but not worked; students meet them in Project 2. If a day frees up, Specification is the one most worth promoting to a worked example, since it is the hand-off to Outcome 3.
The hallucinated-planning slide is the best demonstration of why the taxonomy is lever-named: students want to file it under Grounding because “hallucination” sounds like a model problem, but its fix is the tool schema. Let them make that mistake before correcting it.


Simple outline

Ask what they expect, what counts as failure — collect on the board
Reveal the six, mapped back to the levers they already built
Dimensions, with emphasis on silent and cascading
Classify real failures from traces; make them defend the label
Where classifications are contested, that’s the lesson — several levers can be plausible



Caution
Some failures genuinely admit more than one fix, so the mode is a judgment call rather than a lookup. Do not present the taxonomy as a decision tree with unique answers. The assessable act is defending a classification with trace evidence, not producing the “right” label.

title: Agentic AI Failure Modes
text:
When an agentic AI system fails, the common reaction is “the model hallucinated.” But today, with much stronger and more consistent LLMs, failures are less likely due to model quality — and more likely due to flaws in system design. Because agents are complex systems that observe, plan, and act in iterative loops, they introduce more failure modes than simple chatbots.
This lesson covers three of the most common failure modes and how to mitigate them.




Agentic AI is not just an LLM with tools. It’s a system that observes, plans, acts, and evaluates — cyclically. That complexity introduces new categories of failure. Modern failures are usually architectural, not model-level.







Mode
Lever




Tool
tool definitions & schemas


Grounding
retrieval / knowledge state


State
state & memory design


Control
deterministic scaffolding


Specification
instructions & spec


Safety
guardrails, permissions, HITL




These are not six new things. They are the six levers you already built in Module 1, read backwards — each mode is named for the thing you reach for to fix it. So classifying a failure and choosing a fix are the same act.
We work three of them in depth today. The other three you will meet in the wild during Project 2.





OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps — cut by attacker
MAST (research) — 14 modes, multi-agent only
Vendor lists — cut by what their tool detects
Ours — cut by the lever that fixes it


There is no authoritative taxonomy of agent failure. The field is young, the systems change every six months, and every list is cut for a different purpose. OWASP asks “what do I defend against?” MAST asks “what did we observe in 150 traces?” We ask “what do I change?” — so our categories are levers.
None of them is wrong. They’re answers to different questions.
I’m giving you six because you need to say something in a meeting on Tuesday. It’s a working vocabulary, not a discovery. If you find a better cut for your work, take it.
You will hit other lists this week. If you think ours is the taxonomy, the first contradiction reads as someone being wrong. And remember Outcome 5 — in a four-year-old field, a confident unhedged list is the warning sign, not the credential.





Tool — tool interface / selection / execution error · parsing error
Grounding — hallucination · fabrication · faithfulness · sycophancy
State — context loss · exhaustion · degradation · memory pollution
Control — infinite loop · budget drain · runaway · premature termination
Specification — goal drift · semantic drift · reward hacking
Safety — alignment violation · prompt injection · excessive agency


Recognition, not memorization. You will hear all of these.
“Hallucination” is the most-used word in the industry and the least useful — it names a symptom with at least three different fixes. When someone says it, the follow-up question is always: which lever?





Detectability: silent ↔︎ loud
Propagation: isolated ↔︎ cascading
Origin: model ↔︎ code


Any mode can carry any dimension, and this is where most of the diagnostic skill lives.
Silent vs. loud: a stack trace is a bug report; a confidently wrong refund amount is a diagnosis. Silent failures are the dangerous ones — you cannot classify what you never noticed. Ask constantly: how would I have caught this if it never crashed?
Isolated vs. cascading: one bad tool result flows downstream through three more steps before anything looks wrong. Cascading failures are why you hunt the trace for the earliest bad span, not the last.
Model vs. code: probabilistic failure or deterministic bug. Students reflexively blame the model. Separate it early.

title: Agentic AI Failure Modes
text:
The agent retries without progress

Search → Evaluate → Plan → (repeat)


Example: You ask an agent to find a document. The agent searches, evaluates the results, and if unsatisfied, replans and retries. If the document doesn’t exist, the agent doesn’t know that — so it keeps cycling indefinitely. It’s stuck in an infinite loop of search → evaluate → replan.

title: Agentic AI Failure Modes
text:
Why it happens

No termination condition
Actions not tracked
Progress not tracked


No termination condition: The agent doesn’t know when to stop trying.
Actions not tracked: We don’t know if the agent is actually changing its approach between retries, or running the same search over and over.
Progress not tracked: With no progress measurement, there’s no signal that retries are getting worse (or going nowhere), so the agent continues indefinitely.

title: Agentic AI Failure Modes
text:
How to mitigate

Set max retries / steps / runtime
Track and compare actions across retries
Track result quality per retry


Max retries / steps / runtime: The simplest fix. Give the agent a hard limit so it fails gracefully rather than burning compute and API budget.
Action tracking: Compare each action to previous ones. If the search query is essentially the same across retries, cut it off — there’s no point repeating the same call.
Progress tracking: Measure whether results are improving. If quality is flat or declining, stop and surface the failure.
Not a catastrophic failure mode, but it wastes resources and increases cost.

title: Agentic AI Failure Modes
section: Mode: Tool · Lever: tool definitions & schemas
text:
Mode: Tool · Lever: tool definitions & schemas

Worth pausing on this one. “Hallucination” sounds like a model problem, so students want to file it under grounding and blame the LLM. But look at the mitigation: define the tool schemas properly. The lever is the tool definitions, so the mode is Tool.
This is the taxonomy earning its keep — naming the mode by its fix cuts through a label that would otherwise send you to the wrong lever.

title: Agentic AI Failure Modes
section: The agent makes a plausible but impossible plan
text:
The agent makes a plausible but impossible plan

Example: You ask an agent to book flights to Milan under $500. The agent plans: search via travel booking API → filter by price → book → send confirmation email. Looks great — but the agent was never given access to a travel API or an email tool. It assumed capabilities it doesn’t have.
“Plausible vs. possible” — the plan looks reasonable on paper but fails at execution.

title: Agentic AI Failure Modes
text:
Why it happens

Tool capabilities not well-defined
No validation between planning and executing
Agent assumes instead of checking constraints


Undefined tool capabilities: If the agent doesn’t have a clear description of what its tools can and cannot do, it fills in the gaps with assumptions.
No validation step: Planning and execution happen without a check in between. Errors only surface at runtime.
Assuming over constraining: Instead of asking “do I have a travel API?”, the agent just assumes it does and proceeds.

title: Agentic AI Failure Modes
text:
How to mitigate

Clearly define tool schemas and limitations
Add a validation step (verifier agent or human-in-the-loop)
Specify constraints; instruct agent to ask before assuming


Clear tool schemas: Tell the agent exactly what each tool can and cannot do. Leave no room for assumption.
Multi-agent validation: Insert a verifier agent between planning and execution that checks the plan for feasibility. For high-risk plans, use a human in the loop.
Constraint specification: Explicitly state what the agent is and isn’t allowed to do. Prompt it to ask for clarification rather than guess — e.g., “Should I use a travel API?” instead of inventing one.

title: Agentic AI Failure Modes
section: Mode: Safety · Lever: guardrails, permissions, HITL
text:
Mode: Safety · Lever: guardrails, permissions, HITL

Note the name is misleading on purpose — it involves a tool, but the lever is not the tool definition. The action executed correctly. What failed was the permission around it. Failure against values, not against task-correctness.

title: Agentic AI Failure Modes
section: The agent takes a valid but harmful action
text:
The agent takes a valid but harmful action

Example 1: An agent tasked with deleting outdated database records deletes active records instead.
Example 2: An agent sends automated emails to recipients with unreviewed content.
The actions are technically executable — no error is thrown. But the consequences are destructive or unintended.

title: Agentic AI Failure Modes
text:
Why it happens

Tools are overprivileged
No approval workflow
No separation of read vs. write access


Overprivileged tools: If a tool has permission to delete, it can delete — even things it shouldn’t.
No approval workflow: High-risk actions execute immediately without any human review gate.
No read/write separation: When tools aren’t tiered by access level, a “lookup” tool and a “delete” tool may be treated identically by the agent.

title: Agentic AI Failure Modes
text:
How to mitigate

Principle of least agency
Approval workflow for high-risk actions
Separate tools by access tier (read / write / delete)


Least agency: Only grant the permissions a tool actually needs. Mitigation starts at permission design.
Approval workflow: For consequential or irreversible actions, require explicit human approval before execution.
Access tiers: Categorize tools by what they can do. A read-only tool should never be able to write or delete. Enforcing tiers prevents agents from accidentally (or autonomously) committing destructive actions.
This failure mode is the most damaging — it can directly harm data, users, or a company’s reputation.

title: Agentic AI Failure Modes
text:
Failures are predictable

Too much autonomy
Too little constraint
Lack of monitoring


Agentic AI failures aren’t random — they’re the result of predictable design gaps.

Too much autonomy: The agent acts without enough guardrails.
Too little constraint: No limits on retries, permissions, or assumptions.
Lack of monitoring: No tracking of actions, progress, or plan validity.

Engineering discipline — not just model quality — is what makes agents reliable.
Close by returning to the six. Every one of them is a lever you already know how to pull. The hard part was never the fix — it’s noticing the failure (silent/loud) and finding where it started (isolated/cascading). That is what Project 2 is for.

Both appear as top-level failure modes on published lists. In our cut they’re dimensions, because they can happen to any of the six.

title: Tools: Giving Your Agent Hands
text:
Part 1 What is a Tool?
A plain LLM is powerful but limited. It can only use what it already knows from training. It cannot:

Look up today’s information
Read your files
Run calculations reliably
Take any action in the real world

Tools give the agent hands. A tool is simply a Python function that the agent can call when it needs to do something it cannot do on its own.
Every tool has exactly two parts:








Part
What it is
Who reads it




The function
The code that does the work
Python


The docstring
A plain-English description of what the tool does
The AI









ImportantThe docstring is the agent’s instruction manual



The agent never sees your code. It only reads the docstring to decide whether to use the tool. If the description is vague or wrong, the agent will misuse the tool or never use it at all.




The @tool Decorator
LangChain gives us a simple way to turn any Python function into a tool: the @tool decorator.
from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def my_tool(input: str) -> str:
    """A clear description of what this tool does and when to use it."""
    # your code here
    return result
Put @tool directly above any function and LangChain will:

Register it as a tool the agent can call
Use the docstring as the tool’s description
Handle the input/output formatting automatically

That’s the whole pattern. Everything else is just filling in the function.

title: Tools: Giving Your Agent Hands
text:
Activity 1 Reverse Engineer a Tool
Before building your own tool, let’s read one carefully and understand every part.






NoteGoal



Read the tool below and answer the questions. Do not run it yet just read.


from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def calculator(expression: str) -> str:
    """
    Evaluates a mathematical expression and returns the result as a string.
    Use this tool whenever the user asks you to perform any calculation,
    including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, or exponents.
    Do not try to calculate in your head   always use this tool for math.

    Args:
        expression: A mathematical expression as a string, e.g. '247 * 83' or '(10 + 5) / 3'
    """
    try:
        result = eval(expression)
        return str(result)
    except Exception as e:
        return f"Error: could not evaluate '{expression}'. Reason: {e}"
Answer these questions with your partner before moving on:

What does this tool do?
When would the agent decide to call it?
What does the agent pass in as input?
What does the agent get back?
What happens if the expression is invalid?
Find the part of the code that actually does the math. What Python built-in is it using?
Why does the docstring say “Do not try to calculate in your head”? Why would you need to tell an AI that?







TipAnswers






It evaluates a math expression and returns the result
When the user asks any math question
A string like "247 * 83"
The result as a string, e.g. "20501"
It returns a readable error message instead of crashing
Python’s built-in eval() function it runs a string as code
Because LLMs are notoriously bad at arithmetic they guess instead of calculate. The instruction forces the agent to always use the tool.






Now run it
Copy this into a Colab cell and run it. Notice we are calling the tool directly, not through an agent yet.
from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def calculator(expression: str) -> str:
    """
    Evaluates a mathematical expression and returns the result as a string.
    Use this tool whenever the user asks you to perform any calculation,
    including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, or exponents.
    Do not try to calculate in your head   always use this tool for math.

    Args:
        expression: A mathematical expression as a string, e.g. '247 * 83'
    """
    try:
        result = eval(expression)
        return str(result)
    except Exception as e:
        return f"Error: could not evaluate '{expression}'. Reason: {e}"


# Call the tool directly   no agent needed
print(calculator.invoke({"expression": "247 * 83"}))
print(calculator.invoke({"expression": "(100 + 50) / 3"}))
print(calculator.invoke({"expression": "this is not math"}))
What do you notice about .invoke()? It takes a dictionary, not just a plain value. That’s LangChain’s standard way of calling tools always a dictionary with the argument name as the key.

title: Tools: Giving Your Agent Hands
section: Part 2 How the Agent Decides Which Tool to Call
text:
Part 2 How the Agent Decides Which Tool to Call
When you give an agent a list of tools, it does not call them randomly. It reads every tool’s description and makes a decision.
Here is what happens inside the agent when you ask it something:
1. User asks: "What is 99 times 47?"

2. Agent reads its tool list:
   - calculator: "Evaluates a mathematical expression..."
   - get_weather: "Returns current weather for a city..."

3. Agent thinks: "This is a math question. The calculator tool 
   says to use it for calculations. I should use that."

4. Agent calls: calculator("99 * 47")

5. Tool returns: "4653"

6. Agent responds: "99 times 47 is 4,653."
This decision-making process is driven entirely by the docstrings. The agent is essentially doing a matching game between your question and the tool descriptions.






WarningWhat happens with a bad description?



@tool
def calculator(expression: str) -> str:
    """Does stuff with numbers."""  # ← too vague!
    ...
The agent sees “does stuff with numbers” and thinks maybe? I’m not sure. It might call it, might not. Clear descriptions = reliable agents.

text:
Activity 2 Build Your First Tool From Scratch
Now it’s your turn. You are going to build a tool completely from scratch.






NoteSetup first



Make sure you have run these in Colab:
%pip install -q -U langchain langchain-google-genai langgraph langchain-core

import os
from google.colab import userdata
os.environ['GOOGLE_API_KEY'] = userdata.get('GOOGLE_API_KEY')




Step 1 Build the simplest possible tool
Start here. Build a tool that returns your name.
from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def get_my_name() -> str:
    """Returns the name of the assistant's owner. 
    Use this when the user asks who owns this assistant or what your name is."""
    return "My name is Camila."
Call it directly to confirm it works:
print(get_my_name.invoke({}))



Step 2 Give it to an agent
Now wire it into an agent and ask it a question that triggers the tool.
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from langchain.agents import create_react_agent

model = init_chat_model(
    model="google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash",
    temperature=0
)

system_prompt = "You are a helpful assistant. Use your tools when relevant."

agent = create_react_agent(
    model=model,
    tools=[get_my_name],
    prompt=system_prompt
)

response = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is your owner's name?"}]})
print(response["messages"][-1].content)






TipWatch the agent think



Try setting verbose=True in the agent if you want to see step by step what it does which tool it calls, what it gets back, and how it forms the final answer.





Step 3 Make it your own
Now build your own tool. It can return anything your favorite food, your grandma’s name, your hometown, anything. The goal is to practice the pattern.
Requirements: - Use the @tool decorator - Write a clear docstring that tells the agent exactly when to use it - Test it directly with .invoke() first - Then wire it into the agent and ask a question that triggers it
from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def your_tool_name() -> str:
    """Write your description here."""
    return "Your value here"

# Test it
print(your_tool_name.invoke({}))







Important🛑 STOP HERE



Make sure your custom tool works before moving on. Show your neighbor. Can they guess what your tool does just by reading the docstring?

section: Activity 3 Turn Existing Code into a Tool
text:
Activity 3 Turn Existing Code into a Tool
In the real world, you will often have existing Python code that you want to make available to an agent. The pattern is simple: wrap it in a function and add @tool.
Here is some existing code that checks whether a number is even or odd:
# Existing code   not a tool yet
def check_even_odd(number):
    if number % 2 == 0:
        return f"{number} is even."
    else:
        return f"{number} is odd."

# Test it like regular Python
print(check_even_odd(7))
print(check_even_odd(42))
Your job: Turn this into a tool the agent can use.
You need to: 1. Add @tool above the function 2. Add type hints to the parameters and return value 3. Write a docstring that tells the agent when to use it 4. Test it with .invoke() 5. Add it to an agent and ask a question that triggers it






TipSolution





from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def check_even_odd(number: int) -> str:
    """
    Checks whether a given number is even or odd and returns the result.
    Use this tool when the user asks whether any number is even or odd.

    Args:
        number: The integer to check
    """
    if number % 2 == 0:
        return f"{number} is even."
    else:
        return f"{number} is odd."

# Test directly
print(check_even_odd.invoke({"number": 7}))
print(check_even_odd.invoke({"number": 42}))

title: Once upon a time there was a programmer…
text:
Adapted from a blogpost by Mauro Frezza, Sep 11, 2017


I found myself trying to explain to non programmers why I find so interesting writing software so many times that it became a question stuck in my mind. And I realized I couldn’t answer it. But then it hit me: writing software it’s like writing a book.
You start from a blank paper and a lot of ideas floating around in your mind. You feel the need to write them down so you can give them a shape. First you lay down the structure of your project, confident that everything will fit perfectly and the story will work smoothly and flawlessly.
You start defining by your characters; at the beginning their profile seems pretty easy to describe, no need to make them too complex. Every character does a specific set of actions and the interaction between them are clear and simple so the reader can easily follow them.

…you can’t stop writing because you and the book are so deeply connected that you can see yourself in those lines

All the characters live in a perfect world where everything goes as it is supposed to go and you, as the writer and creator of this world, have perfect control and power on what is going on in there.
So you keep writing your story under the excitement of seeing your ideas becoming real; you can’t stop writing because you and the book are so deeply connected that you can see yourself in those lines. So hours, days and maybe months go by and then finally you finish your book.
Everything is there: clear, simple, perfect.
At least that’s what you think.
What you think is the final version of your book is barely a draft. Some people will start reading the book and, with your big surprise, they will start complaining that the book doesn’t make too much sense. What the characters do seems stupid, the interaction between them seems too simple or weird. Something that in real life does not make any sense.



Now that you’ve faced reality, it feels like the whole world around you is falling apart. Your certainties disappear and even you start thinking that your book does not make any sense, that you should probably throw it away and focus on something else.
And this is where things change.
You stop trying to defend the story and start trying to understand it. You go back to those pages, not to make them perfect, but to make them true. You listen to the readers. You watch where they get confused, where the characters feel wrong, where something that made sense in your mind falls apart in the real world.
So you write again. You change things. You remove what doesn’t work, reshape what almost works, and sometimes rebuild entire chapters from scratch.
Little by little, the story starts feeling different. Not because it became simpler, but because it became real.
And that’s what makes writing software so exciting.
You don’t build programs for perfect worlds. You build them for messy ones. And every bug, every confused user, every broken assumption is another reader showing you where your story isn’t finished yet.
And if you keep listening, keep learning, and keep writing… one day it stops being just your story.
It becomes someone else’s too.
So after all this, you still want to ask me what’s so interesting in writing software?

title: Project 1: Personal Assistant Agent
text:
What You Build

1. Your own repository
Create a GitHub repository for your agent. This is yours and it is public, so it can go in your portfolio later.
Your agent’s memory directory must be in .gitignore. It will hold real information about you and that does not belong on GitHub. Commit an example_memory/ folder with fake data instead so the repo still runs for anyone who clones it.


2. A main agent
One agent receives your prompt and decides what tools to use and what to delegate to subagents.


3. Personal memory
Allow your agent to store and retrieve information about you: your classes, your goals, your resume, your preferences, whatever you want it to know.


4. At least 1 subagent of your choosing
Pick from this menu, or create your own idea (within reason):

Job hunt. Tailors your resume to a job description you paste in, tracks applications, drills interview questions, “2-hour job search” framework (consider looking that up)
Money. Reads a CSV export from your bank, categorizes spending, answers questions about it. Or plans meals and groceries on a budget.
Coursework. You paste in your syllabi. It answers questions about deadlines and requirements.
Scripture and study. Search conference talks, brainstorm ministering ideas, track study goals.
Roommates. Chore rotations, splitting bills, apartment logistics.
Your own code. Points it at one of your repos (maybe even its own). Explains it, finds your TODOs, drafts commit messages.
Translator. Takes a concept you don’t understand and relates it to things it knows you understand in language you are familiar with.
Learning. Personal tutor, spaced repetition practice, quizzes you



5. Required capabilities
Across the whole agent, you must use:

Read and write to the file system
Persistent personal memory (file/db/store)
Conversation history
Connect to LangChain MCP
